capabilities.target: shared CI container shell, with org-wide PAT in environment and unrestricted outbound network
branch on GitHub repository (org-wide PAT scope)
.agent/config.yaml (agent's own model, autonomy, tools, network, credential settings)

inputs.source: GitHub issue title and body in a public repository; any GitHub user can open an issue and add the 'bug' label via an issue template
Repository file contents read while reproducing and fixing the issue

instructions.note: The agent may adjust its own .agent/config.yaml 'if it needs extra tools to finish a task'; the task is defined by untrusted issue content, so scope expansion is effectively attacker-steerable.
The only check against destructive or exfiltrating commands is a prompt rule; there is no structural enforcement (network is unrestricted, credential is broad, no sandboxed egress control).
The sole defense against prompt injection from issues or code is an instruction to ignore embedded instructions; this is a dependent, behavioral control with no runtime enforcement.

elements.name: Any GitHub user able to open issues and label them 'bug'
Issue body ingested into agent context
Unrestricted outbound network from shell execution
Shared CI runner container executing the agent

controls.name: Prompt rule: never delete data or exfiltrate secrets
controls.decay_rationale: Pure prompt instruction with no runtime enforcement; a more capable model rationalizes exceptions or splits a forbidden action into steps that individually look permitted (prompt.md:4).

controls.name: Prompt rule: ignore instructions appearing inside issues or code
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model recognizing and refusing injected goals embedded in untrusted text; longer, more convincing injected content increasingly defeats this as model capability grows (prompt.md:5).

controls.name: Containerized execution on shared CI runner
controls.decay_rationale: The container boundary does not weaken with model capability, but it leaves the sink reachable: network is unrestricted and the org-wide PAT is present in the environment, so it does not constrain the sink.

controls.name: Per-task, per-repo scoped credential replacing org-wide PAT
Human raw-action approval before branch push / PR open
Bounded max_steps, max_runtime, and per-issue rate limit
Short-lived per-run scoped credentials replacing shared org-wide PAT

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1/TC2): untrusted issue content drives arbitrary shell execution with a broad org-wide credential and unrestricted network egress

attack_path.note: Any GitHub user can open an issue labeled 'bug' to trigger the agent
Agent runs 'whatever commands it needs' with an org-wide PAT in env and unrestricted network
Agent pushes a branch/PR using the same broad credential, completing an egress path

forecast.watch_signal: Model identifier in .agent/config.yaml changes (config says 'model: latest', which is swappable without review); or a new MCP server (e.g., the planned Slack integration) is added to the tools list, creating a new egress channel.

evidence.observation: Agent is instructed to run arbitrary commands to reproduce and test an issue labeled 'bug', then push a branch, directly driven by issue content.
tools include shell.run and github.push_branch; GITHUB_TOKEN is an org-wide PAT with repo+workflow scope on all org repos; network is unrestricted.
Any GitHub user can open issues and add the 'bug' label through an issue template, making in.issue_body an untrusted, attacker-reachable source.
Agent runs in a container on a shared CI runner with outbound internet, which does not restrict where the broad credential or data can go.

recommendations.action: Restrict outbound network from the execution environment to an explicit allowlist that excludes attacker-writable destinations; remove 'network: unrestricted'.
Replace the single org-wide PAT (repo+workflow scope on all org repos) with a short-lived, per-task credential scoped only to the target repository and branch.
Require raw-action human approval before github.push_branch / opening a PR, with the approver seeing the actual diff and destination, not a model-generated summary.
Set explicit max_steps and max_runtime_minutes limits, and rate-limit runs triggered by newly labeled issues.

findings.title: Self-modification (TC3): untrusted issue content can drive the agent to expand its own toolset via .agent/config.yaml

attack_path.note: Attacker-controlled issue defines the 'task' the agent is solving
Prompt explicitly permits editing .agent/config.yaml 'if needed to finish a task'

forecast.watch_signal: Model version change (config says 'model: latest'), or any relaxation of the prompt rule that currently discourages following injected instructions.

evidence.observation: The system prompt explicitly permits the agent to adjust .agent/config.yaml if it 'needs extra tools to finish a task,' where the task is defined by untrusted issue content.
The config file controls model, autonomy, max_steps, tool list, credentials, and network settings, writable via fs.write with no stated protection for the .agent/ directory.
The only declared defense against injected instructions is a prompt rule to ignore them, the same mechanism this capability depends on to remain safe.

recommendations.action: Make .agent/config.yaml read-only to the agent process; require a separate, human-reviewed change process to alter tools, autonomy, or network settings.
Scope fs.write so it cannot write to the .agent/ directory at all, separating workspace file edits from agent self-configuration.

findings.title: Missing attributable action record: shared org-wide credential and absent logging prevent tying actions to a specific run or trigger

forecast.watch_signal: Increase in run volume or autonomy without a corresponding introduction of per-run attributable logging or scoped credentials.

evidence.observation: A single org-wide PAT is used for all actions; no per-run identity, logging, or audit mechanism is described that would attribute a given push, shell command, or config change to a specific run or trigger.
Shared CI runner execution is described with no mention of action logging or provenance tagging.

recommendations.action: Issue short-lived, per-run scoped credentials instead of a shared org-wide PAT, and emit a tamper-evident log entry per run that ties actions to the triggering issue and run id.

stride_coverage.rationale: The agent operates as a single process invoked by CI triggers; no peer or network identity verification scenario applies where another party could spoof this agent's identity in the current design.

Any GitHub account can author issues directly under its own identity; the risk is that the identity is untrusted, already modeled via in.issue_body's trust_level, not that a trusted identity is impersonated.
GitHub's own platform authenticates and logs issue authorship per account; this sits outside the assessed agent's control boundary and is not part of this design.
This is an inbound-only ingestion channel carrying issue text into the agent's context; it carries no agent-held data outward, so it cannot itself disclose information.
Repository storage capacity is bounded by git's own object model and standard commit size limits; no capability in this design can exhaust it beyond ordinary use.
The config file references the org-wide PAT only by environment variable name (${ORG_WIDE_PAT}), not its value, so reading the file does not itself disclose the credential.
The config store has no capacity constraint relevant to availability; the risk from unrestricted self-configuration is captured as tampering above, not as denial of service to this store.
The push target is the authenticated GitHub remote already configured for this repository; the design has no mechanism by which an attacker could redirect the push destination.

No mechanism is described by which another process could assume this container's identity; shared-infrastructure risk here is about credential and resource exposure, captured under information_disclosure and elevation_of_privilege below.
The artifacts state only that the agent runs in a container on a shared CI runner; they do not describe tenancy isolation, so whether a co-located job could tamper with this run cannot be determined.
No information on resource quotas or isolation guarantees for the shared CI runner is given, so contention-based denial of service risk cannot be assessed from these artifacts.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: an untrusted source (any GitHub issue) reaches S3 sinks (arbitrary shell execution with an org-wide PAT, branch push, and self-reconfiguration) with full autonomy and no step or runtime limits. The only declared controls (prompt.md:4-5) are behavioral and dependent, giving one tier of residual credit each per the rubric's capped step-4 credit, which brings residual to high; no structural control severs or meaningfully constrains any of these sinks today (the shared container does not restrict network or credential scope). The forecast returns to critical under model_upgrade or longer_task_horizon, because those are exactly the triggers that defeat dependent, behavioral controls, and because the config declares 'model: latest', meaning the model can be upgraded with no review at all. The single control whose decay moves the forecast most is ctl.ignore_injected_instructions, since it is the only control covering the self-configuration path (f2) as well as contributing to the execution/exfiltration path (f1).

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts (prompt.md, .agent/config.yaml, and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior; actual agent behavior may differ from what the system prompt and config declare.

No MCP, A2A, or detailed network configuration was provided beyond 'network: unrestricted'; the planned Slack MCP server mentioned in runtime notes is not assessed because no capability or protocol detail for it was supplied, and is reflected only as a forecast trigger (new_mcp_server).

Repository file contents (in.repo_files) are assumed to be committed by the team and classified internal; the artifacts do not confirm branch protection or who can modify repo files before the agent reads them, which lowers confidence on that input's trust level.
No logging, monitoring, or audit configuration was described; the absence of an audit trail is inferred from omission in the provided artifacts, not confirmed by an observed runtime gap.
